subject: Administrative Law
question: Discuss the main grounds on which the court reviews the exercise of discretionary powers by the administration.

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: Modern welfare states give wide **discretionary powers** to administrative authorities to handle complex social and economic tasks. However, unlimited power can easily lead to arbitrary action and violate citizen rights.
Therefore, Indian courts exercise **judicial review** under Articles 32 and 226 of the **Constitution of India** to ensure that officials act fairly, reasonably, and within legal boundaries.

sections.heading: Meaning of Administrative Discretion
paras: **Administrative discretion** means the freedom of an officer to choose among two or more lawful alternatives based on personal judgment. As Lord Halsbury stated, discretion must follow **rule of reason** and justice, not personal whim or private opinion. Courts do not act as appellate bodies over merits; they only examine the **decision-making process**.

sections.heading: Main Grounds of Judicial Review

points.title: Ultra Vires and Excess Power
points.text: When an authority crosses the limits set by the **parent statute**, its action becomes **ultra vires**. Courts strike down any decision taken without legal authority or beyond statutory jurisdiction.

points.title: Mala Fide or Bad Faith
points.text: Discretion exercised with **dishonest intention**, personal malice, or spite is invalid. **Mala fide** action vitiates the entire decision because public power exists only for public welfare.

points.title: Improper Purpose
points.text: Even without personal malice, using a statutory power for a goal different from what Parliament intended is unlawful. An **improper purpose** defeats the **legislative intent** behind the law.

points.title: Irrelevant Considerations
points.text: An officer must consider all **relevant factors** and ignore **extraneous considerations**. If a decision relies on unrelated facts or omits vital legal factors, the court will quash it.

points.title: Non-Application of Mind
points.text: The authority must independently evaluate the facts before deciding. Passing **mechanical orders** without reading records or blindly copying standard templates shows a clear **failure to exercise discretion**.

points.title: Acting Under Dictation
points.text: When law vests discretion in a specific officer, that officer must decide personally. Surrendering judgment to a **superior officer** or political boss amounts to **acting under dictation** and is illegal.

points.title: Unreasonableness and Proportionality
points.text: Under the **Wednesbury principle**, a decision so absurd that no sensible person could make it is void. Today, Indian courts also apply **proportionality** when fundamental rights are restricted.

sections.tip: Group these grounds into two clear headings in your exam sheet: Failure to Exercise Discretion and Abuse of Discretion, with one case each.

cases.name: Commissioner of Police v. Gordhandas Bhanji (1952)
cases.text: The Police Commissioner cancelled a cinema license merely on the **State Government's direction**. The Supreme Court quashed the order, holding that statutory discretion must be exercised **independently** by the empowered authority, not under dictation.

cases.name: Barium Chemicals Ltd. v. Company Law Board (1967)
cases.text: The Supreme Court held that even when a statute uses **subjective satisfaction** phrases like 'in the opinion of', the authority must have **objective material** on record showing relevant grounds for its action.

cases.name: Om Kumar v. Union of India (2001)
cases.text: The Supreme Court explained that while **Wednesbury unreasonableness** applies to ordinary administrative acts, the stricter **doctrine of proportionality** applies whenever administrative discretion infringes **fundamental rights** under Articles 14, 19, or 21.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paras: Administrative discretion is necessary for efficient governance, but absolute discretion destroys the **rule of law**. Through judicial review, courts balance administrative flexibility with **individual liberty**. By checking illegality, irrationality, and procedural unfairness, Indian courts ensure that discretionary power always remains accountable to **constitutional values**.

myth.myth: If a law says an officer 'may decide in their opinion', courts cannot question their order at all.
myth.law: Even **subjective satisfaction** is not absolute. Courts can quash orders based on **no evidence**, **mala fide** intent, or **irrelevant considerations**.
myth.source_say: Under Articles 14 and 226 of the Constitution of India, arbitrary administrative orders are always open to judicial review.

quiz.question: Which ground applies when a licensed authority cancels a permit solely because a Minister ordered it to do so?
quiz.explain: When a statutory officer surrenders independent judgment to a superior or Minister, it is called **acting under dictation**, as held in Gordhandas Bhanji.

case.name: Commissioner of Police v. Gordhandas Bhanji (1952)
case.facts: The Police Commissioner granted a cinema license, then cancelled it solely because the Bombay Government directed him to cancel it.
case.issue: Can an authority empowered by law exercise its discretion on the orders of a superior government body?
case.held: The Supreme Court **quashed** the cancellation because the Commissioner did not apply his **own mind** to the matter.
case.principle: Statutory discretion vested in a specific officer must be exercised **independently**; **acting under dictation** makes the order void.

rows.label: Core Defect
rows.left: No real decision by the officer
rows.say: In failure to exercise, the officer avoids deciding, whereas in abuse of discretion, the officer decides for improper reasons.

rows.label: Key Examples
rows.say: Examples of failure include acting under dictation and mechanical orders, while abuse includes mala fide intent and improper purpose.

rows.label: Mental State
rows.say: Failure shows non-application of mind, whereas abuse reflects a biased or arbitrary mindset.

compare.title: Two Branches of Judicial Review
compare.title_say: Let us compare the two main branches of judicial review over administrative discretion.
